claim: The neural crest (NC) is a multipotent embryonic cell population.
source: The neural crest (NC) is an important multipotent embryonic cell population and its impaired specification leads to various developmental defects, often in an anteroposterior (A-P) axial level-specific manner.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the neural crest that is part of established scientific knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Impaired neural crest specification leads to various developmental defects in an anteroposterior axial level-specific manner.
source: The neural crest (NC) is an important multipotent embryonic cell population and its impaired specification leads to various developmental defects, often in an anteroposterior (A-P) axial level-specific manner.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field of developmental biology and neurocristopathies.

claim: Trunk NC cells are derived from neuromesodermal-potent progenitors of the postcranial body.
source: Recent studies have indicated that trunk NC cells, the presumed precursors of childhood tumour neuroblastoma, are derived from neuromesodermal-potent progenitors of the postcranial body.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies mentioned in the abstract.

claim: TBXT mediates early posterior NC/spinal cord regionalisation together with WNT signalling effectors.
source: We show that TBXT, a pro-mesodermal transcription factor, mediates early posterior NC/spinal cord regionalisation together with WNT signalling effectors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBXT-driven chromatin remodelling occurs via its binding in key enhancers within HOX gene clusters and other posterior regulator-associated loci.
source: This occurs by TBXT-driven chromatin remodelling via its binding in key enhancers within HOX gene clusters and other posterior regulator-associated loci.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A second phase of trunk HOX gene control marks the differentiation of NMPs toward their TBXT-negative NC/spinal cord derivatives and relies predominantly on FGF signalling.
source: This initial posteriorisation event is succeeded by a second phase of trunk HOX gene control that marks the differentiation of NMPs toward their TBXT-negative NC/spinal cord derivatives and relies predominantly on FGF signalling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from signalling pathway perturbation experiments.

claim: Neural crest cells emerge at all levels of the anteroposterior axis.
source: NC cells emerge at all levels of the anteroposterior (A-P) axis and their A-P position determines the identity of their derivatives
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: The A-P position of neural crest cells determines the identity of their derivatives.
source: NC cells emerge at all levels of the anteroposterior (A-P) axis and their A-P position determines the identity of their derivatives
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology supported by citations.

claim: Cranial NC produces mesoectodermal cell types (e.g. dermis, cartilage, and bone), melanocytes, neurons, and glial cells colonising the head.
source: cranial NC produces mesoectodermal cell types (e.g. dermis, cartilage, and bone), melanocytes, neurons, and glial cells colonising the head
evidence: This is established knowledge about cranial neural crest derivatives, supported by citations (Le Douarin et al., 2004; Rocha et al., 2020; Rothstein et al., 2018).

claim: Vagal NC cells arise between somites 1 and 7.
source: vagal NC cells, arising between somites 1 and 7, contribute (together with their sacral counterparts emerging at axial levels posterior to somite 28) predominantly to the enteric nervous system
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about vagal neural crest location.

claim: Vagal NC cells contribute predominantly to the enteric nervous system.
source: vagal NC cells, arising between somites 1 and 7, contribute (together with their sacral counterparts emerging at axial levels posterior to somite 28) predominantly to the enteric nervous system
evidence: This is established knowledge about vagal neural crest derivatives, supported by citations.

claim: Sacral NC cells emerge at axial levels posterior to somite 28.
source: vagal NC cells, arising between somites 1 and 7, contribute (together with their sacral counterparts emerging at axial levels posterior to somite 28) predominantly to the enteric nervous system
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about sacral neural crest location.

claim: Cardiac NC is a subpopulation of vagal NC that generates various heart structures.
source: vagal NC cells, arising between somites 1 and 7, contribute (together with their sacral counterparts emerging at axial levels posterior to somite 28) predominantly to the enteric nervous system and include a subpopulation (termed cardiac NC) that generates various heart structures
evidence: This is established knowledge about cardiac neural crest, supported by citations.

claim: Trunk NC generates dorsal root/sympathetic neurons, adrenal chromaffin cells, and melanocytes.
source: trunk NC generates dorsal root/sympathetic neurons, adrenal chromaffin cells, and melanocytes (reviewed in Le Douarin et al., 2004; Rocha et al., 2020; Rothstein et al., 2018)
evidence: This is established knowledge about trunk neural crest derivatives, supported by citations.

claim: Defects in the specification, differentiation, or migration of NC cells lead to neurocristopathies.
source: Defects in the specification, differentiation, or migration of NC cells (known collectively as neurocristopathies) lead to a wide spectrum of serious developmental disorders, often in an axial level-specific manner (Pilon, 2021; Vega-Lopez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neurocristopathies often occur in an axial level-specific manner.
source: Defects in the specification, differentiation, or migration of NC cells (known collectively as neurocristopathies) lead to a wide spectrum of serious developmental disorders, often in an axial level-specific manner (Pilon, 2021; Vega-Lopez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms directing the acquisition of distinct A-P axial identities by human NC cells remain largely undefined.
source: However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms directing the acquisition of distinct A-P axial identities by human NC cells remain largely undefined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The A-P patterning of the vertebrate embryonic body relies on the coordinated action of Hox gene family members.
source: In vivo, the A-P patterning of the vertebrate embryonic body and its nascent cellular components relies on the coordinated action of Hox gene family members (arranged as paralogous groups [PG] in four distinct chromosomal clusters: A, B, C, and D).
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Hox genes are arranged as paralogous groups in four distinct chromosomal clusters: A, B, C, and D.
source: In vivo, the A-P patterning of the vertebrate embryonic body and its nascent cellular components relies on the coordinated action of Hox gene family members (arranged as paralogous groups [PG] in four distinct chromosomal clusters: A, B, C, and D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox gene organization.

claim: Transcriptional activation of Hox genes is initiated during gastrulation in mammals.
source: In mammals, transcriptional activation of Hox genes is initiated during gastrulation, within the posterior part of the embryo around the primitive streak and proceeds in a sequential manner reflecting their 3'-to-5' genomic order, a phenomenon described as temporal collinearity or the Hox clock (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017; Dollé et al., 1989; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hox gene activation proceeds in a sequential manner reflecting their 3'-to-5' genomic order.
source: In mammals, transcriptional activation of Hox genes is initiated during gastrulation, within the posterior part of the embryo around the primitive streak and proceeds in a sequential manner reflecting their 3'-to-5' genomic order, a phenomenon described as temporal collinearity or the Hox clock (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017; Dollé et al., 1989; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about temporal collinearity, supported by citations.

claim: The sequential activation of Hox genes is described as temporal collinearity or the Hox clock.
source: In mammals, transcriptional activation of Hox genes is initiated during gastrulation, within the posterior part of the embryo around the primitive streak and proceeds in a sequential manner reflecting their 3'-to-5' genomic order, a phenomenon described as temporal collinearity or the Hox clock (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017; Dollé et al., 1989; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established terminology in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The Hox clock continues to operate after gastrulation until the end of somitogenesis.
source: The Hox clock continues to operate after gastrulation, until the end of somitogenesis, in the posterior growth zone comprising the caudal lateral epiblast-late primitive streak, and later the tail bud (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017; Wymeersch et al., 2019; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The colinear activation of Hox genes in the posterior growth region is coupled to the assignment of terminal A-P coordinates of cell lineages that make up the postcranial axis.
source: The colinear activation of Hox genes in the posterior growth region is thought to be tightly coupled to the assignment of the terminal A-P coordinates of the cell lineages that make up the postcranial axis, including the NC (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017; Wymeersch et al., 2019; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a model supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Anterior cranial NC is Hox-negative.
source: In the case of NC, anterior cranial NC is Hox-negative, posterior cranial NC cells express Hox PG(1-3) genes, while vagal NC cells are marked by the expression of Hox PG(3-5) members and positivity for Hox PG(5-9) genes denotes a trunk NC character (Rocha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox expression patterns in neural crest, supported by citation.

claim: Posterior cranial NC cells express Hox PG(1-3) genes.
source: In the case of NC, anterior cranial NC is Hox-negative, posterior cranial NC cells express Hox PG(1-3) genes, while vagal NC cells are marked by the expression of Hox PG(3-5) members and positivity for Hox PG(5-9) genes denotes a trunk NC character (Rocha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox expression patterns in neural crest, supported by citation.

claim: Vagal NC cells are marked by the expression of Hox PG(3-5) members.
source: In the case of NC, anterior cranial NC is Hox-negative, posterior cranial NC cells express Hox PG(1-3) genes, while vagal NC cells are marked by the expression of Hox PG(3-5) members and positivity for Hox PG(5-9) genes denotes a trunk NC character (Rocha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox expression patterns in neural crest, supported by citation.

claim: Positivity for Hox PG(5-9) genes denotes a trunk NC character.
source: In the case of NC, anterior cranial NC is Hox-negative, posterior cranial NC cells express Hox PG(1-3) genes, while vagal NC cells are marked by the expression of Hox PG(3-5) members and positivity for Hox PG(5-9) genes denotes a trunk NC character (Rocha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox expression patterns in neural crest, supported by citation.

claim: The post-gastrulation posterior growth zone is marked by high levels of WNT/FGF signalling activity.
source: The post-gastrulation posterior growth zone is marked by high levels of WNT/FGF signalling activity and harbours a pool of multipotent axial progenitors driving embryonic axis elongation in a head-tail direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the posterior growth zone, supported by citations in the context.

claim: The posterior growth zone harbours multipotent axial progenitors driving embryonic axis elongation.
source: The post-gastrulation posterior growth zone is marked by high levels of WNT/FGF signalling activity and harbours a pool of multipotent axial progenitors driving embryonic axis elongation in a head-tail direction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the posterior growth zone.

claim: NMPs generate a large fraction of the spinal cord and presomitic/paraxial mesoderm.
source: These include neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) that generate a large fraction of the spinal cord as well as presomitic/paraxial mesoderm, the building blocks of the musculoskeleton (reviewed in Henrique et al., 2015; Wymeersch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMP derivatives, supported by citations.

claim: NMPs are marked by the co-expression of Sox2 and Brachyury (T).
source: NMPs are marked by the co-expression of neural and mesodermal genes, such as those encoding the transcription factors Sox2 and Brachyury (T) (Guillot et al., 2021; Henrique et al., 2015; Martin and Kimelman, 2012; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Tsakiridis et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMP markers, supported by citations.

claim: NMPs express posteriorly expressed genes such as Nkx1-2, Cdx2, Tbx6, and Hox family members.
source: NMPs are marked by the co-expression of neural and mesodermal genes, such as those encoding the transcription factors Sox2 and Brachyury (T) (Guillot et al., 2021; Henrique et al., 2015; Martin and Kimelman, 2012; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Tsakiridis et al., 2014), as well as a number of other posteriorly expressed genes such as Nkx1-2, Cdx2, Tbx6, and Hox family members (Amin et al., 2016; Dias et al., 2020; Gouti et al., 2017; Guillot et al., 2021; Javali et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2017; Rodrigo Albors et al., 2018; Wymeersch et al., 2019; Young et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMP gene expression, supported by citations.

claim: Trunk NC cells are derived from NMPs.
source: Fate mapping, lineage tracing, and single-cell transcriptomics studies in vertebrate embryos have revealed that trunk NC cells, which give rise to neuroblastoma (the most common extracranial solid tumour in infants) following oncogenic transformation, are derived from NMPs (Javali et al., 2017; Lukoseviciute et al., 2021; Shaker et al., 2021; Tzouanacou et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to fate mapping and lineage tracing studies.

claim: Trunk NC cells give rise to neuroblastoma following oncogenic transformation.
source: Fate mapping, lineage tracing, and single-cell transcriptomics studies in vertebrate embryos have revealed that trunk NC cells, which give rise to neuroblastoma (the most common extracranial solid tumour in infants) following oncogenic transformation, are derived from NMPs (Javali et al., 2017; Lukoseviciute et al., 2021; Shaker et al., 2021; Tzouanacou et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumour in infants.
source: Fate mapping, lineage tracing, and single-cell transcriptomics studies in vertebrate embryos have revealed that trunk NC cells, which give rise to neuroblastoma (the most common extracranial solid tumour in infants) following oncogenic transformation, are derived from NMPs (Javali et al., 2017; Lukoseviciute et al., 2021; Shaker et al., 2021; Tzouanacou et al., 2009; Wymeersch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: In vitro generation of trunk NC cells from hPSCs relies on the induction of an NMP-like intermediate following WNT/FGF signalling stimulation.
source: Moreover, recent work has demonstrated that the in vitro generation of trunk NC cells and their derivatives from hPSCs relies on the induction of an NMP-like intermediate following stimulation of WNT/FGF signalling pathways (Abu-Bonsrah et al., 2018; Faustino Martins et al., 2020; Frith et al., 2018; Frith and Tsakiridis, 2019; Hackland et al., 2019; Kirino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: A generic posterior axial identity is installed early within NMP precursors of trunk NC cells under the influence of WNT/FGF activities.
source: These and other studies have pointed to a model where a generic posterior axial identity is installed early within the NMP precursors of trunk NC cells under the influence of WNT/FGF activities prior to their differentiation and commitment to an NC fate (Frith et al., 2018; Metzis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lateral-most caudal epiblast domain in mouse embryos is marked by T (Brachyury) expression at E8.75-E9.0.
source: We confirmed by wholemount immunofluorescence analysis that, similar to their human in vitro counterparts, the LE domain in mouse is also marked by expression of T (Brachyury) immediately before the time of early posterior NC emergence (embryonic day [E] 8.75–E9.0, Theiler stage [TS] 13–14) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Low-level expression of Tfap2a was first detected within the posterior LE domain from E9.0.
source: Low-level expression of Tfap2a, potentially marking nascent NC cells (Mitchell et al., 1991; Rothstein and Simoes-Costa, 2020), was first detected within the posterior LE domain from E9.0 (Figure 1 Bg-h vs Bc-d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and citations.

claim: Committed NC cells express Sox9 alongside Tfap2a.
source: 'Committed' NC cells, located anteriorly at the same time points, were found to also express Sox9 alongside Tfap2a (Figure 1 Ba-b and Be-f).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: T-positive embryonic cells contribute to the posterior neural tube and trunk NC.
source: These data demonstrate that NC-fated axial progenitors in the mouse embryo exhibit T expression in line with the previous lineage tracing studies showing that T-positive embryonic cells contribute to the posterior neural tube and trunk NC (Anderson et al., 2013; Mugele et al., 2018; Shaker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lineage tracing studies.

claim: Tetracycline addition induced a considerable reduction in TBXT expression at the transcript and protein level in hESC-derived NMPs.
source: We confirmed that Tet addition induced a considerable reduction in TBXT expression both at the transcript and protein level compared to untreated controls (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: 346 genes were significantly upregulated in TBXT knockdown NMPs compared to untreated controls.
source: We found that 346 and 293 genes were significantly up- and down-regulated respectively in TBXT knockdown cells compared to untreated controls (padj<0.05, Wald test; log2FC>|0.5|; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 293 genes were significantly downregulated in TBXT knockdown NMPs compared to untreated controls.
source: We found that 346 and 293 genes were significantly up- and down-regulated respectively in TBXT knockdown cells compared to untreated controls (padj<0.05, Wald test; log2FC>|0.5|; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Most differentially expressed genes following TBXT knockdown were established regulators of A-P regionalisation/posterior development.
source: Gene ontology (GO) biological processes enrichment analysis revealed that most differentially expressed genes were established regulators of A-P regionalisation/posterior development (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TBXT knockdown triggered a significant reduction in the expression of various HOX genes belonging to anterior, central, and posterior PG(1-9).
source: Moreover, we found that TBXT knockdown triggered a significant reduction in the expression of various HOX genes belonging to anterior, central, and posterior PG(1-9) (Figure 2G, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The most highly upregulated genes following TBXT knockdown included anterior visceral endoderm/endoderm, anterior neurectoderm, and pluripotency/early post-implantation epiblast-associated genes.
source: On the contrary, the most highly upregulated genes included anterior visceral endoderm (AVE)/endoderm, anterior neurectoderm, and pluripotency/early post-implantation epiblast-associated genes such as SOX17, LEFTY1/2, OTX2, CER1, HHEX, NANOG, and GDF3 (Figure 2F, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TBXT knockdown severely impairs the induction of NMPs and their immediate presomitic mesoderm progenitor derivatives from hPSCs.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that TBXT knockdown severely impairs the induction of NMPs and their immediate presomitic mesoderm progenitor derivatives from hPSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq and qPCR data presented.

claim: TBXT directs the establishment of a posteriorising signalling environment associated with early HOX gene activation upon pluripotency exit.
source: They also suggest that TBXT directs the establishment of a posteriorising signalling environment associated with early HOX gene activation, upon pluripotency exit, since in its absence hPSCs adopt an identity that resembles the anterior epiblast despite the combined presence of caudalising WNT (CHIR) and FGF (FGF2) signalling agonists.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing upregulation of anterior markers and downregulation of posterior markers.

claim: The expression of most HOX PG(1-9) genes was dramatically reduced in Tet-treated trunk NC cultures compared to untreated controls.
source: We found that the expression of most HOX PG(1-9) genes examined was dramatically reduced in the resulting Tet-treated cultures compared to their untreated counterparts (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The failure of TBXT-depleted NMPs to properly induce HOX gene expression persists in their NC derivatives.
source: We found that the expression of most HOX PG(1-9) genes examined was dramatically reduced in the resulting Tet-treated cultures compared to their untreated counterparts (Figure 3B and C) indicating that the failure of TBXT-depleted NMPs to properly induce HOX gene expression persists in their NC derivatives.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qPCR data from trunk NC cultures.

claim: CDX2 expression levels were severely decreased in TBXT-depleted trunk NC cultures.
source: The expression levels of CDX2, an NMP/spinal cord/early trunk NC regulator (Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2016; Sanchez-Ferras et al., 2012) were also found to be severely decreased (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A statistically significant reduction in SOX10 and PAX3 transcript levels was observed in Tet-treated trunk NC cultures.
source: A statistically significant reduction in the levels of some NC-associated transcripts such as SOX10 and PAX3 was observed in the presence of Tet (p<0.05 and p<0.01 respectively; paired t-test; Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No change in SOX10 protein levels was detected following TBXT knockdown in trunk NC cultures.
source: A statistically significant reduction in the levels of some NC-associated transcripts such as SOX10 and PAX3 was observed in the presence of Tet (p<0.05 and p<0.01 respectively; paired t-test; Figure 3D) though no change in SOX10 protein levels was detected (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The acquisition of a posterior axial identity by trunk NC cells is shaped by the action of TBXT.
source: Based on these data we conclude that the acquisition of a posterior axial identity by trunk NC cells is shaped by the action of TBXT, an NMP/pro-mesodermal regulator.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced HOX gene expression following TBXT knockdown.

claim: Early (days 0-3) Tet treatment resulted in a statistically significant decrease in the number of cells co-expressing SOX1 and HOXC9 proteins.
source: However, we observed a statistically significant decrease in the number of cells co-expressing SOX1 and HOXC9 proteins (denoting a CNS posterior spinal cord identity) in the case of cultures treated with Tet between days 0 and 3 compared to their untreated counterparts (from ~10 to ~1%; p<0.05, paired t-test) (Figure 4C; compare dark blue bars in the middle graph in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Continuous (days 0-7) TBXT knockdown decreased the mean percentage of SOX10+ cells from ~23 to ~3.6%.
source: A more pronounced effect of continuous (days 0–7) TBXT knockdown on both SOX10 transcript and protein levels was also detected: the mean percentage of SOX10+ cells decreased from ~23 to ~3.6% (p<0.05, paired t-test)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis.

claim: Continuous (days 0-7) TBXT knockdown decreased the mean percentage of SOX10+HOXC9+ cells from ~20 to ~1%.
source: the mean percentage of SOX10+HOXC9+ cells decreased from ~20 to ~1% (p<0.05, paired t-test; Figure 4B and C; compare purple bars in the top graph in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Early Tet treatment (days 0-3) resulted in global downregulation of all HOX genes examined as well as CDX2.
source: The sharp decline in HOXC9 protein positivity linked to early Tet treatment (Figure 4C and D) was accompanied by a global downregulation in the expression of all HOX genes examined by quantitative PCR (qPCR) as well as CDX2 (Figure 4B and E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Late days 3-7 Tet treatment had a minimal effect on HOX/CDX2 transcription.
source: On the contrary, late days 3–7 Tet treatment had a minimal effect on HOX/CDX2 transcription (Figure 4B and E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: TBXT exerts its effect on posterior axial identity acquisition at an early stage that temporally coincides with the induction of NMPs from pluripotent cells.
source: Moreover, our results indicate that TBXT exerts its effect on these processes at an early stage that temporally coincides with the induction of NMPs from pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal Tet treatment experiments showing that early treatment has the most pronounced effect.

claim: TBXT knockdown in day 3 FGF-CHIR-treated cultures resulted in concomitant downregulation of WNT targets and upregulation of WNT antagonists.
source: Our RNA-seq data revealed the concomitant downregulation of WNT targets and upregulation of WNT antagonists (e.g. DKK4) in day 3 FGF-CHIR-treated cultures in the presence of Tet (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The inability of TBXT-depleted NC cells to activate HOX genes may be linked to an early reduction in WNT activity.
source: Our RNA-seq data revealed the concomitant downregulation of WNT targets and upregulation of WNT antagonists (e.g. DKK4) in day 3 FGF-CHIR-treated cultures in the presence of Tet (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2F) suggesting that the inability of TBXT-depleted NC cells to activate HOX genes may be linked to an early reduction in WNT activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing changes in WNT signaling components.

claim: TBXT knockdown-triggered reduction of HOX gene expression in NC cultures was accompanied by a significant reduction in the expression of WNT signalling target genes such as TCF1, LEF1, and CDX2.
source: This is further supported by our observation that TBXT knockdown-triggered reduction of HOX gene expression in our NC cultures was also accompanied by a significant reduction in the expression of WNT signalling target genes such as TCF1, LEF1, and CDX2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: WNT signalling stimulation alone, in the absence of FGF activity, rescued the induction of most HOX genes and TBXT/CDX2 with variable efficiency.
source: However, WNT signalling stimulation alone, in the absence of any FGF activity, rescued the induction of most HOX genes and TBXT/CDX2 with variable efficiency (Figure 5D, red bars)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from signaling perturbation experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: WNT is the main instructive pathway controlling global HOX transcription and the expression of major axis elongation regulators during the differentiation of hPSCs toward NMPs.
source: However, WNT signalling stimulation alone, in the absence of any FGF activity, rescued the induction of most HOX genes and TBXT/CDX2 with variable efficiency (Figure 5D, red bars) indicating that WNT is the main instructive pathway controlling global HOX transcription and the expression of major axis elongation regulators during the differentiation of hPSCs toward NMPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the signaling perturbation experiments.

claim: HOXC gene activation was found to be equally dependent on WNT and FGF signalling.
source: The HOXC genes were an exception, as their activation was found to be equally dependent on WNT and FGF signalling (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from signaling perturbation experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: WNT signalling inhibition in the presence of BMP activity resulted in a statistically significant reduction in the expression of many HOX gene family members during NMP differentiation to trunk NC.
source: Treatment of differentiating NMPs with XAV to inhibit WNT signalling in combination with BMP stimulation resulted in a statistically significant reduction in the expression of many of the HOX gene family members examined albeit to a lesser degree compared to days 0–3 (Figure 5G, dark blue vs purple bars).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from signaling perturbation experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: WNT signalling attenuation in the presence of BMP activity led to a moderate increase in the expression of anterior NC markers (OTX2 and ETS1) and a decrease in posterior NC markers (CDX2).
source: WNT signalling attenuation in the presence of BMP activity also led to a moderate increase in the expression of anterior (OTX2 and ETS1) and a decrease in posterior (CDX2) NC markers while the levels of neural/NC-specific transcripts appeared unaffected (Figure 5F, dark blue vs purple bars).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: WNT stimulation in combination with BMP inhibition resulted in significant upregulation in the expression of most HOX genes relative to WNT-BMP controls.
source: On the contrary, WNT stimulation in combination with the BMP inhibitor LDN193189 (LDN) resulted in significant upregulation in the expression of most HOX genes relative to the WNT-BMP controls (Figure 5G, light blue vs purple bars)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: WNT stimulation with BMP inhibition resulted in the complete extinction of SOX10 expression and a concomitant increase in SOX1 expression.
source: Moreover, this treatment resulted in the complete extinction of the expression of the definitive NC marker SOX10 and a concomitant increase in the CNS neural progenitor marker SOX1 both at the transcript and protein levels (Figure 5F, light blue vs purple bars; the percentage of SOX1 + cells increased from 0.7 to 45%, p<0.05 paired t-test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1, compare dark blue bars in the graph in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMP signalling steers NMPs toward an NC fate at the expense of a spinal cord neurectoderm identity.
source: Moreover, this treatment resulted in the complete extinction of the expression of the definitive NC marker SOX10 and a concomitant increase in the CNS neural progenitor marker SOX1 both at the transcript and protein levels (Figure 5F, light blue vs purple bars; the percentage of SOX1 + cells increased from 0.7 to 45%, p<0.05 paired t-test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1, compare dark blue bars in the graph in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) pointing to a role for BMP signalling in steering NMPs toward an NC fate at the expense of a spinal cord neurectoderm identity, in agreement with previous observations (Leung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HOX gene activation in hPSC-derived NMPs and its coupling to early programming of posterior axial identity in NMP-derived NC cells are primarily driven by a WNT-TBXT regulatory loop.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that HOX gene activation in hPSC-derived NMPs and its tight coupling to the early programming of a posterior axial identity in NMP-derived NC cells are primarily driven by a WNT-TBXT regulatory loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signaling perturbation and TBXT knockdown experiments.

claim: The early dependence of HOX gene expression on WNT signalling diminishes with time as NMPs gradually differentiate toward NC.
source: However, the early dependence of HOX gene expression on WNT signalling diminishes with time as NMPs gradually differentiate toward NC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal signaling perturbation experiments.

claim: The highest levels of WNT activity in mouse embryos at E8.75-E9.0 were confined within the T+ posterior growth region.
source: In agreement with previous work (Ferrer-Vaquer et al., 2010), the highest levels of WNT activity were confined within the T+ posterior growth region (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of R26-WntVis reporter embryos shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and citation to previous work.

claim: NC-fated regions within the T+ lateral-most caudal epiblast domain are marked by higher WNT signalling levels compared to more rostral epiblast positions.
source: Wholemount immunostaining followed by 3D modelling of the high anti-GFP (a-GFP)-positive fraction (a-GFPhigh) demonstrated that NC-fated regions within the T+ lateral-most caudal epiblast domain are marked by higher WNT signalling levels compared to more rostral epiblast positions (dashed lines in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining and 3D modeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Early specification of NM-potent T+ trunk NC progenitors correlates with high WNT activity.
source: These findings further confirm that early specification of NM-potent T+ trunk NC progenitors correlates with high WNT activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the WntVis reporter analysis in mouse embryos.

claim: The association between NC specification and WNT activity becomes less prevalent as cells gradually commit to a definitive NC fate.
source: However, this association becomes less prevalent as cells gradually commit to a definitive NC fate in line with our in vitro observations showing the progressively decreasing WNT-dependence of TBXT-driven posterior axial identity programming in NC cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo and in vitro data.

claim: The levels of most HOX transcripts were largely unaffected in day 7 pre-neural spinal cord progenitors generated from TBXT-depleted cells with continuous Tet treatment.
source: The levels of most HOX transcripts examined were largely unaffected in day 7 pre-neural spinal cord progenitors generated from TBXT-depleted cells and similar to untreated controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Low levels of TBXT transcripts were detected in control pre-neural spinal cord cultures, comparable to Tet-treated counterparts.
source: In line with our previous observations and published in vivo data (Gofflot et al., 1997; Nordström et al., 2006; Wind et al., 2021), we also detected low levels of TBXT transcripts in control cultures, and surprisingly, these were comparable to their Tet-treated counterparts (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and citations to previous work.

claim: Selection of cells evading shRNA knockdown and maintaining low levels of TBXT may occur upon culture in pre-neural spinal cord cell-promoting culture conditions.
source: This finding suggests that selection of cells evading shRNA knockdown and maintaining low levels of TBXT may occur upon culture in pre-neural spinal cord cell-promoting culture conditions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of similar TBXT levels in control and Tet-treated cultures.

claim: Later addition of Tet on day 3 restored efficient TBXT knockdown in pre-neural spinal cord cultures.
source: Later addition of Tet on day 3, at the start of NMP differentiation toward pre-neural spinal cord cells, appeared to restore efficient TBXT knockdown (Figure 6D and F)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and F.

claim: Late Tet addition (day 3) had no major impact on HOX PG(1-9) gene expression or the levels of early spinal cord/pre-neural transcripts in day 7 pre-neural spinal cord cultures.
source: Later addition of Tet on day 3, at the start of NMP differentiation toward pre-neural spinal cord cells, appeared to restore efficient TBXT knockdown (Figure 6D and F) but, again, had no major impact on either HOX PG(1-9) gene expression or the levels of the early spinal cord/pre-neural transcripts CDX2 and NKX1-2 in the resulting day 7 cultures (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: HOX expression dynamics/posterior axial identity in NMP-derived pre-neural spinal cord progenitors generated under WNT/high FGF signalling are largely unaffected by TBXT depletion.
source: These results indicate that HOX expression dynamics/posterior axial identity in NMP-derived, pre-neural spinal cord progenitors, generated under the influence of WNT/high FGF signalling activity, are largely unaffected by TBXT depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the qPCR data from TBXT knockdown experiments in pre-neural spinal cord cultures.

claim: The combined presence of extrinsic WNT/FGF signals compensates for reduced TBXT levels, rescuing the effects of its knockdown on HOX gene expression in 'neutral' culture conditions.
source: They also suggest that the combined presence of extrinsic WNT/FGF signals compensates for the reduced levels of TBXT, rescuing the effects of its knockdown on HOX gene expression in 'neutral' culture conditions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the effects of TBXT knockdown in different culture conditions.

claim: WNT signalling inhibition in the presence of FGF activity during days 3-7 does not have a major effect on HOX or CDX2 transcript levels in pre-neural spinal cord progenitors.
source: We found that WNT signalling inhibition in the presence of FGF activity during this time window does not appear to have a major effect on HOX or CDX2 transcript levels (blue vs grey bars in Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from signaling perturbation experiments shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Blocking FGF signalling in combination with CHIR treatment resulted in a dramatic reduction in the expression of most HOX genes, particularly those belonging to PG(4-9), as well as CDX2.
source: In contrast, blocking FGF signalling in combination with CHIR treatment resulted in a dramatic reduction in the expression of most HOX genes examined, particularly those belonging to PG(4-9), as well as CDX2 (red bars vs grey bars, Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from signaling perturbation experiments shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: FGF signalling attenuation in the presence of CHIR results in the elimination of SOX2+HOXC9+ pre-neural spinal cord populations.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis further revealed that FGF signalling attenuation in the presence of CHIR results in the elimination of SOX2+HOXC9+ (their mean percentage decreased from ~45 to ~9%; n=3 p<0.05 paired t-test; Figure 7D, compare purple bars in the graph in Figure 7E) and CDX2+HOXC9+ pre-neural spinal cord populations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7D, E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Maintenance of posterior axial identity in NMP-derived pre-neural early spinal cord cells is driven primarily by FGF signalling.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that maintenance of a posterior axial identity in NMP-derived pre-neural early spinal cord cells is driven primarily by FGF signalling, which gradually becomes functionally equivalent to TBXT in controlling trunk HOX gene/CDX2 expression as NMP differentiation progresses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the signaling perturbation experiments in pre-neural spinal cord cultures.

claim: 24,704 TBXT-binding regions were identified in NMPs by ChIP-seq.
source: We identified 24,704 TBXT-binding regions in NMPs (Supplementary file 3, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: A large fraction of TBXT-binding regions were located within introns (~50%) and distal intergenic (~38%) regions.
source: a large fraction of which were located within introns (~50%) and distal intergenic (~38%) regions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A small number (n=2088) of non-overlapping TBXT binding sites was detected in undifferentiated hESCs.
source: A small number (n=2088) of non-overlapping TBXT binding sites was also detected in undifferentiated hESCs, in line with the reported low-level expression of this transcription factor in mesoderm-biased pluripotent cells (Stavish et al., 2020; Tsakiridis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and citations to previous work.

claim: Target genes associated with TBXT binding sites around the transcriptional start site were predominantly linked to developmental regulators of A-P regionalisation.
source: The GO biological processes enrichment analysis of target genes associated with TXBT binding sites around the transcriptional start site (–2000 to +500 bp; 3084 peaks, 2841 genes) revealed an over-representation of established developmental regulators of A-P regionalisation (Benjamini–Hochberg padj <0.05; Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TBXT binding regions in hPSC-derived NMPs were enriched for the Brachyury consensus binding motif and other T-box binding motifs such as EOMES and TBX6.
source: Transcription factor motif enrichment analysis revealed that the TBXT binding regions in hPSC-derived NMPs were enriched, as expected, for the Brachyury consensus binding motif as well as other T-box binding motifs such as EOMES and TBX6 (Figure 8A, Supplementary file 5)
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Other over-represented motifs in TBXT binding regions included WNT signalling effectors (LEF1/TCF3) and Homeobox genes such as CDX factors (CDX2/4) and various HOX family members.
source: Other over-represented motifs included WNT signalling effectors (LEF1/TCF3) and Homeobox genes such as CDX factors (CDX2/4) and various HOX family members (Figure 8A, Supplementary file 5)
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The majority (~85%) of downregulated genes following TBXT knockdown were directly bound by TBXT.
source: Comparison of TBXT ChIP-seq targets with our list of differentially expressed genes following Tet-induced TBXT knockdown in day 3 FGF-CHIR treated cultures (Figure 2) revealed that the majority (~85%) of the downregulated (padj <0.05, log2FC>|1|) genes, including HOX PG(1-9) members, pro-mesodermal factors and WNT-FGF signalling components, were directly bound by TBXT, while most (~60%) of their upregulated counterparts were not (Figure 8B, C and F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8B, C, F.

claim: Most (~60%) of upregulated genes following TBXT knockdown were not directly bound by TBXT.
source: Comparison of TBXT ChIP-seq targets with our list of differentially expressed genes following Tet-induced TBXT knockdown in day 3 FGF-CHIR treated cultures (Figure 2) revealed that the majority (~85%) of the downregulated (padj <0.05, log2FC>|1|) genes, including HOX PG(1-9) members, pro-mesodermal factors and WNT-FGF signalling components, were directly bound by TBXT, while most (~60%) of their upregulated counterparts were not (Figure 8B, C and F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8B, C, F.

claim: TBXT acts primarily as a transcriptional activator of key downstream NMP/mesoderm regulators and HOX genes.
source: This indicates that TBXT acts primarily as a transcriptional activator of key downstream NMP/mesoderm regulators and HOX genes as previously reported in the mouse (Amin et al., 2016; Beisaw et al., 2018; Guibentif et al., 2021; Koch et al., 2017; Lolas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data integration, supported by citations to previous work in mouse.

claim: 4421 regions corresponding to loss of chromatin accessibility were detected following TBXT knockdown in NMPs.
source: We detected 4421 and 4027 unique regions corresponding to loss or gain of chromatin accessibility (a readout of DNA regulatory element/enhancer activity) following Tet treatment, respectively (distance from TSS ranging from –1–1 kb, log2FC cutoff = 2 and p-value<0.05; Figure 8D, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: 4027 regions corresponding to gain of chromatin accessibility were detected following TBXT knockdown in NMPs.
source: We detected 4421 and 4027 unique regions corresponding to loss or gain of chromatin accessibility (a readout of DNA regulatory element/enhancer activity) following Tet treatment, respectively (distance from TSS ranging from –1–1 kb, log2FC cutoff = 2 and p-value<0.05; Figure 8D, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Genes associated with loss of chromatin accessibility following TBXT knockdown were predominantly linked to A-P patterning, mesoderm specification, and WNT signalling.
source: Genes associated with loss of chromatin accessibility were predominantly linked to A-P patterning, mesoderm specification, and WNT signalling (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: The Tet-induced downregulation of most TBXT target transcripts was accompanied by a significant loss of 'open' chromatin regions within the TBXT binding sites.
source: Moreover, the Tet-induced downregulation of most transcripts found to be TBXT targets (Supplementary file 3) was also accompanied by a significant loss of 'open' chromatin regions within the TBXT binding sites (Figure 8E and F, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8E and F.

claim: Loss of chromatin accessibility following TBXT knockdown occurred within sites dispersed within all HOX clusters as well as key presomitic mesoderm regulators and WNT signalling components.
source: These included sites that were dispersed within all HOX clusters as well as key presomitic mesoderm regulators (e.g. TBX6 and MSGN1) and WNT signalling components (e.g. WNT3A/8 A and LEF1; Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There was no obvious correlation between upregulation of expression following TBXT knockdown and chromatin accessibility change.
source: On the contrary, there was no obvious correlation between upregulation of expression following TBXT knockdown and chromatin accessibility change (Figure 8E, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by integration of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Gain of accessible regions in TBXT-depleted NMPs occurred predominantly within/around loci linked to neural development.
source: Gain of accessible regions in TBXT-depleted hPSC-derived NMPs appeared to occur predominantly within/around loci linked to neural development (e.g. SOX3 and DLG2; Tao et al., 2003; Wood and Episkopou, 1999), most of which were not bound directly by TBXT (Figure 8G, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8G and citations.

claim: ATAC-seq sites marked by loss of chromatin accessibility following TBXT knockdown were uniquely enriched in CDX, T-box factor and HOX binding-associated DNA sequence elements.
source: Moreover, examination of transcription factor binding motifs (annotated using HOMER; Heinz et al., 2010; Benjamini–Hochberg padj<0.05) showed that ATAC-seq sites marked by loss of chromatin accessibility following TBXT knockdown were uniquely enriched in CDX, T-box factor and HOX binding-associated DNA sequence elements whereas the regions marked by a gain of chromatin accessibility were mainly characterised by motifs indicating binding of SOX, OCT/POU, and Forkhead family transcription factors (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Regions marked by gain of chromatin accessibility following TBXT knockdown were mainly characterised by motifs indicating binding of SOX, OCT/POU, and Forkhead family transcription factors.
source: Moreover, examination of transcription factor binding motifs (annotated using HOMER; Heinz et al., 2010; Benjamini–Hochberg padj<0.05) showed that ATAC-seq sites marked by loss of chromatin accessibility following TBXT knockdown were uniquely enriched in CDX, T-box factor and HOX binding-associated DNA sequence elements whereas the regions marked by a gain of chromatin accessibility were mainly characterised by motifs indicating binding of SOX, OCT/POU, and Forkhead family transcription factors (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Key loci associated with posterior patterning such as HOX clusters and CDX2 were marked by a significant loss of 'open' chromatin regions in TBXT knockdown trunk NC cultures.
source: Further ATAC-seq analysis of trunk NC cells generated from hESC-derived NMPs in the continuous presence (from days 0–8) and absence of Tet revealed that, like in NMPs, various key loci associated with posterior patterning such as HOX clusters and CDX2 were marked by a significant loss of 'open' chromatin regions in TBXT knockdown cultures (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data from trunk NC cultures shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: A major disruption of the chromatin accessibility landscape within/around WNT/BMP/FGF signalling-linked genes was detected in Tet-treated trunk NC cells.
source: We also detected a major disruption of the chromatin accessibility landscape within/around WNT/BMP/FGF signalling-linked genes in Tet-treated trunk NC cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C,D; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data from trunk NC cultures shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Some affected WNT/BMP signaling components, such as WNT1 and BMP7, play a pivotal role in trunk NC specification and delamination.
source: Some affected components of these pathways, such as WNT1 and BMP7, have been shown to play a pivotal role in trunk NC specification and delamination (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2004; Nguyen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many of the disrupted chromatin accessibility regions in trunk NC were bound by TBXT and exhibited reduced chromatin accessibility already at the NMP stage.
source: Many of the disrupted regions, particularly HOX-associated enhancers, were bound by TBXT and exhibited reduced chromatin accessibility already at the NMP stage (see boxed areas in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq data from NMPs and trunk NC shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A loss of trunk NC-specific accessible regions was observed that were not direct TBXT genomic targets in NMPs.
source: However, we also observed a loss of trunk NC-specific accessible regions, which were not direct TBXT genomic targets in NMPs (marked by red asterisks in Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: No major changes in chromatin accessibility were detected in Tet-treated day 7 early spinal cord cultures compared to untreated controls.
source: No major changes in chromatin accessibility were detected in Tet-treated day 7 early spinal cord cultures compared to untreated controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data from early spinal cord cultures shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: TBXT actively reconfigures the chromatin landscape in HOX clusters and other axis elongation-associated loci by direct binding to key enhancer elements.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that TBXT actively reconfigures the chromatin landscape in HOX clusters and other axis elongation-associated loci including WNT signalling components, by direct binding to key enhancer elements to promote the acquisition of a posterior axial character/mesoderm identity during the transition of pluripotent cells toward an NMP state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data.

claim: Some TBXT-controlled NMP-specific 'posteriorisation' enhancers remain active at later stages in TBXT-negative trunk NC derivatives of NMPs.
source: Some of these TBXT-controlled, NMP-specific 'posteriorisation' enhancers appear to remain active at later stages, in TBXT-negative trunk NC derivatives of NMPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data from NMPs and trunk NC.

claim: Trunk NC-specific enhancers are influenced indirectly by TBXT, possibly through its binding and regulation of critical upstream transcription factors or signalling specifiers of NC fate.
source: Moreover, our data also demonstrate the existence of trunk NC-specific enhancers that are influenced indirectly by TBXT, possibly through its binding and regulation of critical upstream transcription factors (e.g. CDX2) or signalling specifiers of NC fate during the early TBXT-positive stages of the transition of NMPs toward trunk NC.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of trunk NC-specific enhancers that are not direct TBXT targets but are affected by TBXT knockdown.

claim: The encoding of a posterior axial identity in human NC/early spinal cord cells relies on their transition through a neuromesodermal progenitor state.
source: Here we provide evidence indicating that the encoding of a posterior axial identity in human NC/early spinal cord cells, embodied by the sequential activation of Hox genes and the induction of posterior markers, relies on their transition through this developmentally plastic entity.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: Primary regionalisation is mediated by TBXT, which together with WNT signalling effectors and possibly CDX2, directs global HOX gene cluster transcription.
source: This 'primary regionalisation' process (Metzis et al., 2018) is mediated by the action of the pro-mesodermal transcription factor TBXT, which, together with WNT signalling effectors and, possibly, CDX2, directs global HOX gene cluster transcription and the expression of posterior/presomitic mesoderm regulators (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data, shown in the model in Figure 9.

claim: The early WNT dependence of HOX expression dynamics diminishes during the transition of NMPs towards their NC/spinal cord derivatives.
source: The early WNT dependence of HOX expression dynamics diminishes during the transition of NMPs towards their NC/spinal cord derivatives; this second phase of HOX gene expression maintenance is in turn controlled predominantly by FGF signalling (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the signaling perturbation experiments, shown in the model in Figure 9.

claim: TBXT influences the adoption of an NC but not CNS spinal cord lineage identity.
source: Our data also revealed another novel role of TBXT, namely its influence on the adoption of an NC but not CNS spinal cord lineage identity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: There exist two distinct phases of posterior axial identity control: an early NMP-based phase involving TBXT/WNT-driven establishment of a HOX-positive posterior character, and a later FGF-based maintenance phase.
source: Collectively, our data reveal a previously unappreciated role for TBXT in prospectively shaping the A-P patterning and specification of NC cells. They also indicate the existence of two distinct phases of posterior axial identity control: (i) an early NMP-based phase that involves the TBXT/WNT-driven establishment/fixing of a HOX-positive, posterior character in uncommitted progenitors, and, (ii) a later one, which is defined by the FGF-based maintenance of a posterior axial identity within the early spinal cord/NC derivatives of NMPs.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.
